title: On Oratory
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi037.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Equidem mihi hoc subsidium iam inde ab adulescentia comparavi, non solum ad causarum usum forensem, sed etiam ad decus atque ornamentum senectutis, ut, cum me vires, quod fere iam tempus adventat, deficere coepissent, ista ab solitudine domum meam vindicarem. Quid est enim praeclarius quam honoribus et rei publicae muneribus perfunctum senem posse suo iure dicere idem, quod apud Ennium dicat ille Pythius Apollo, se esse eum, unde sibi, si non populi et reges, at omnes sui cives consilium expetant, summarum rerum incerti: quos ego ope mea†ex incertis certos compotesque consili dimitto, ut ne res temere tractent turbidas:
passages.english: For my part, I have provided myself with this resource ever since my youth, not only for the practical use of cases in the forum, but also for the honour and adornment of old age, so that, when my strength had begun to fail me (a time that is now almost upon us), I might by this means protect my house from loneliness. For what is more splendid than that an old man who has discharged public offices and duties of state should be able to say by his own right the same thing that Pythian Apollo says in Ennius, that he is the one from whom, if not peoples and kings, at least all his fellow citizens seek counsel, uncertain about the gravest matters: "whom by my help I send away from uncertain certain and possessed of counsel, so that they may not handle troubled affairs rashly":
passages.notes: The edition marks a crux (†) before "ex incertis" in the quotation from Ennius. "ista" (by this means) is taken to refer to the interpretation of the law mentioned just before.

passages.original: Mihi vero inquit Mucius satis superque abs te videtur istorum studiis, si modo sunt studiosi, esse factum; nam, ut Socratem illum solitum aiunt dicere perfectum sibi opus esse, si qui satis esset concitatus cohortatione sua ad studium cognoscendae percipiendaeque virtutis; quibus enim id persuasum esset, ut nihil mallent esse se, quam bonos viros, eis reliquam facilem esse doctrinam;
passages.english: "To me, indeed," said Mucius, "you seem to have done enough and more than enough for the enthusiasms of these young men, provided only that they are really enthusiastic. For, as they say that the famous Socrates used to say that his work was complete if someone had been sufficiently roused by his exhortation to the pursuit of knowing and grasping virtue; for those who had been persuaded that they wished to be nothing more than good men found the rest of learning easy;

passages.original: pupillum filium ipse paene in umeros suos extulisset, qui patris clarissimi recordatione et memoria fletum populo moveret, et duos filios suos parvos tutelae populi commendasset ac se, tamquam in procinctu testamentum faceret sine libra atque tabulis, populum Romanum tutorem instituere dixisset illorum orbitati. Itaque, cum et invidia et odio populi tum Galba premeretur, hisce eum tragoediis liberatum ferebat; quod item apud Catonem scriptum esse video, nisi pueris et lacrimis usus esset, poenas eum daturum fuisse. Haec Rutilius valde vituperabat et huic humilitati dicebat vel exsilium fuisse vel mortem anteponendam.
passages.english: he had all but carried on his own shoulders the orphaned son of his relative Gaius Sulpicius Galus, so that by the recollection and memory of his most illustrious father the boy might move the people to tears, and he had commended his own two small sons to the guardianship of the people, and had said that, as though he were making a will under arms on the eve of battle, without scales or tablets, he was appointing the Roman people guardian of their orphanhood. And so, although Galba was at that time weighed down by both the ill will and the hatred of the people, [Rutilius] used to say that he was set free by these theatrics; and I see that the same thing is written in Cato too, that had he not made use of the boys and of tears, he would have paid the penalty. Rutilius strongly censured these things and used to say that exile, or even death, should have been preferred to such abasement.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the text before the passage has "Q.", which together with "pupillum filium" refers to Quintus, son of Gaius Sulpicius Galus. "In procinctu" refers to the soldier's will made in battle array; "sine libra atque tabulis" alludes to the formal will by bronze and scales (per aes et libram) and written tablets.

passages.original: erat enim Athenis reo damnato, si fraus capitalis non esset, quasi poenae aestimatio; et sententia cum iudicibus daretur, interrogabatur reus, quam quasi aestimationem commeruisse se maxime confiteretur. Quod cum interrogatus Socrates esset, respondit sese meruisse ut amplissimis honoribus et praemiis decoraretur et ut ei victus cotidianus in Prytaneo publice praeberetur, qui honos apud Graecos maximus habetur.
passages.english: For at Athens, when a defendant had been convicted, if the offence was not capital, there was a kind of assessment of the penalty; and when the verdict was being given to the judges, the defendant was asked what assessment, so to speak, he would most readily admit he had deserved. When Socrates had been asked this, he replied that he had deserved to be honoured with the most ample honours and rewards, and to have his daily food provided at public expense in the Prytaneum, which is held to be the highest honour among the Greeks.

passages.original: Nec vero te, carissime frater atque optime, rhetoricis nunc quibusdam libris, quos tu agrestis putas, insequor ut erudiam; quid enim tua potest esse oratione aut subtilius aut ornatius? Sed sive iudicio, ut soles dicere, sive, ut ille pater eloquentiae de se Isocrates scripsit ipse, pudore a dicendo et timiditate ingenua quadam refugisti, sive, ut ipse iocari soleo, unum putasti satis esse non modo in una familia rhetorem, sed paene in tota civitate, non tamen arbitror tibi hos libros in eo fore genere, quod merito propter eorum, qui de dicendi ratione disputarunt, ieiunitatem bonarum artium possit inludi;
passages.english: Nor, my dearest and best brother, am I now pursuing you with some rhetorical books, which you think uncouth, in order to instruct you; for what could be more subtle or more elegant than your own speech? But whether it was by judgement, as you are accustomed to say, or, as that father of eloquence Isocrates wrote of himself, from modesty and a certain well-bred timidity that you shrank from public speaking, or, as I myself am accustomed to joke, you thought that one orator was enough, not only in a single family but almost in the whole state, I do not think, all the same, that these books will be of the kind that could deservedly be mocked because of the poverty in the liberal arts of those who have discussed the theory of speaking;

passages.original: Lucilius, homo doctus et perurbanus, dicere solebat ea, quae scriberet neque se ab indoctissimis neque a doctissimis legi velle, quod alteri nihil intellegerent, alteri plus fortasse quam ipse; de quo etiam scripsit Persium non curo legere,—hic fuit enim, ut noramus, omnium fere nostrorum hominum doctissimus—Laelium Decumum volo, quem cognovimus virum bonum et non inlitteratum, sed nihil ad Persium; sic ego, si iam mihi disputandum sit de his nostris studiis, nolim equidem apud rusticos, sed multo minus apud vos;
passages.english: Gaius Lucilius, a learned and very witty man, used to say that he wished what he wrote to be read neither by the most unlearned nor by the most learned, because the former would understand nothing, the latter perhaps more than he himself; on which point he even wrote: "I do not care to have Persius read [me]" (for he was, as we knew, almost the most learned of all our countrymen), "I want Laelius Decumus", whom we knew as a good man and not unlettered, but nothing compared to Persius. So I, if I now had to discuss these studies of ours, would not wish [to do so] before country bumpkins, but much less before you;
passages.notes: "C." from the text before the passage completes "Gaius Lucilius". The quoted line is from Lucilius. "Laelium Decumum" is the reading given here; some editions read "Decimum".

passages.original: Ea mihi videntur aut in lite oranda aut in consilio dando esse posita; nam illud tertium, quod et a Crasso tactum est et, ut audio, ille ipse Aristoteles, qui haec maxime inlustravit, adiunxit, etiam si opus est, minus est tamen necessarium.Quidnam? inquit Catulus; an laudationes? Id enim video poni genus tertium.
passages.english: These seem to me to lie either in pleading a lawsuit or in giving counsel; for that third [kind], which was both touched on by Crassus and, as I hear, added by Aristotle himself, who shed most light on these matters, is less necessary, even if it is useful. "What is that?" said Catulus. "Eulogies? For I see that this is set down as the third kind."

passages.original: Plane inquit Catulus adsentior.Age vero, inquit Antonius qualis oratoris et quanti hominis in dicendo putas esse historiam scribere?Si, ut Graeci scripserunt, summi, inquit Catulus; si, ut nostri, nihil opus est oratore; satis est non esse mendacem.Atqui, ne nostros contemnas, inquit Antonius, Graeci quoque ipsi sic initio scriptitarunt, ut noster Cato, ut Pictor, ut Piso;
passages.english: "I entirely agree," said Catulus. "Come now," said Antonius, "what sort of orator, and how great a man in speaking, do you think it takes to write history?" "If [it is written] as the Greeks wrote it, the greatest," said Catulus; "if as our people do, there is no need of an orator; it is enough not to be a liar." "And yet, so that you do not despise our own writers," said Antonius, "the Greeks themselves too at first wrote in this way, like our Cato, like Pictor, like Piso;

passages.original: Denique etiam a philosophia profectus princeps Xenophon, Socraticus ille, post ab Aristotele Callisthenes, comes Alexandri, scripsit historiam, et is quidem rhetorico paene more; ille autem superior leniore quodam sono est usus, et qui illum impetum oratoris non habeat, vehemens fortasse minus, sed aliquanto tamen est, ut mihi quidem videtur, dulcior.
passages.english: Finally, setting out from philosophy too, there was first Xenophon, that disciple of Socrates, and afterwards, from the school of Aristotle, Callisthenes, the companion of Alexander, who wrote history, and he indeed in an almost rhetorical manner; the earlier one, however, used a gentler tone, and, as one who lacks that vigorous drive of the orator, he is perhaps less forceful, but nevertheless, as it seems to me at least, considerably more pleasing.

passages.original: Antiquissimi fere sunt, quorum quidem scripta constent, Pericles atque Alcibiades et eadem aetate Thucydides, subtiles, acuti, breves, sententiisque magis quam verbis abundantes: non potuisset accidere, ut unum genus esset omnium, nisi aliquem sibi proponerent ad imitandum. Consecuti sunt hos Critias, Theramenes, Lysias: multa Lysiae scripta sunt; non nulla Critiae; de Theramene audimus; omnes etiam tum retinebant illum Pericli sucum, sed erant paulo uberiore filo.
passages.english: Almost the most ancient, at least of those whose writings are established as genuine, are Pericles and Alcibiades, and of the same age Thucydides: subtle, sharp, concise, and richer in thoughts than in words. It could not have happened that all of them had one style unless they set someone before themselves to imitate. These were followed by Critias, Theramenes, Lysias: there are many writings of Lysias; some of Critias; of Theramenes we hear [only]. All of them still retained that sap of Pericles, but were of a somewhat fuller texture.
passages.notes: "Filo" (thread, texture) is a metaphor for style.

passages.original: sed eorum partim in pompa, partim in acie inlustres esse voluerunt. Atque et illi, Theopompi, Ephori, Philisti, Naucratae multique alii naturis differunt, voluntate autem similes sunt et inter sese et magistri; et hi, qui se ad causas contulerunt, ut Demosthenes, Hyperides, Lycurgus, Aeschines, Dinarchus aliique complures, etsi inter se pares non fuerunt, tamen omnes sunt in eodem veritatis imitandae genere versati, quorum quam diu mansit imitatio, tam diu genus illud dicendi studiumque vixit;
passages.english: but of these some wished to be distinguished in the parade, others in the battle line. And both those men, the Theopompuses, Ephoruses, Philistuses, Naucrateses and many others, differ in their natures but are alike in their aims, both among themselves and with their master; and those who devoted themselves to lawsuits, such as Demosthenes, Hyperides, Lycurgus, Aeschines, Dinarchus and very many others, although they were not equal to one another, nevertheless all worked in the same kind of imitation of reality; and as long as the imitation of them lasted, so long did that kind of speaking and that pursuit live on;
passages.notes: The master is Isocrates (the text before the passage). "In pompa... in acie": display oratory versus real contests.

passages.original: postea quam exstinctis his omnis eorum memoria sensim obscurata est et evanuit, alia quaedam dicendi molliora ac remissiora genera viguerunt. Inde Demochares, quem aiunt sororis filium fuisse Demostheni; tum Phalereus ille Demetrius omnium istorum mea sententia politissimus, aliique horum similes exstiterunt. Quae si volemus usque ad hoc tempus persequi, intellegemus, ut hodie etiam Alabandensem illum Meneclem et eius fratrem Hieroclem, quos ego audivi, tota imitetur Asia, sic semper fuisse aliquem, cuius se similis plerique esse vellent.
passages.english: after these men had died out, all memory of them was gradually dimmed and vanished, and certain other softer and more relaxed kinds of speaking flourished. Then came Demochares, who they say was the son of Demosthenes' sister; then that Demetrius of Phalerum, in my opinion the most polished of all of them, and others like these arose. If we choose to follow these down to the present time, we shall understand that, just as today all Asia imitates that Menecles of Alabanda and his brother Hierocles, whom I have heard, so there has always been someone whom most people wished to resemble.

passages.original: Tum Catulus est, inquit ut dicis, Antoni, ut plerique philosophi nulla tradant praecepta dicendi et habeant paratum tamen quid de quaque re dicant; sed Aristoteles, is, quem ego maxime admiror, posuit quosdam locos, ex quibus omnis argumenti via non modo ad philosophorum disputationem, sed etiam ad hanc orationem, qua in causis utimur, inveniretur; a quo quidem homine iam dudum, Antoni, non aberrat oratio tua, sive tu similitudine illius divini ingeni in eadem incurris vestigia sive etiam illa ipsa legisti atque didicisti, quod quidem mihi magis veri simile videtur;
passages.english: Then Catulus said: "It is as you say, Antonius, that most philosophers hand down no rules of speaking and yet have ready what to say on any subject; but Aristotle, the man I admire most, set out certain topics from which every line of argument might be found, not only for the disputation of philosophers but also for this oratory which we use in lawsuits; and indeed your discourse, Antonius, has for some time not strayed from that man, whether through a likeness to that divine genius you fall into the same tracks, or whether you have actually read and learned those very things, which indeed seems to me more probable;

passages.original: Minime, inquit Antonius; ac sic decrevi philosophari potius, ut Neoptolemus apud Ennium paucis: nam omnino haud placet. Sed tamen haec est mea sententia, quam videbar exposuisse: ego ista studia non improbo, moderata modo sint: opinionem istorum studiorum et suspicionem artifici apud eos, qui res iudicent, oratori adversariam esse arbitror, imminuit enim et oratoris auctoritatem et orationis fidem.
passages.english: "Not at all," said Antonius; "and I have decided to philosophise rather as Neoptolemus does in Ennius: 'a little, for wholly it does not please [me].' But still this is my view, which I thought I had set out: I do not disapprove of those studies, provided they are moderate; but I consider that a reputation for those studies, and a suspicion of art, among those who judge the case, is damaging to an orator, for it diminishes both the orator's authority and the credibility of the speech."

passages.original: Fieri nullo modo potuit. Saepe enim audivi poetam bonum neminem—id quod a Democrito et Platone in scriptis relictum esse dicunt—sine inflammatione animorum exsistere posse et sine quodam adflatu quasi furoris. Qua re nolite existimare me ipsum, qui non heroum veteres casus fictosque luctus velim imitari atque adumbrare dicendo neque actor sim alienae personae, sed auctor meae, cum mihi M’.
passages.english: It could in no way have happened. For I have often heard that no one can be a good poet (and this, they say, was left in writing by Democritus and Plato) without a kindling of the mind and without a certain inspiration, as it were, of frenzy. Therefore do not suppose that I myself, who have no wish to imitate and sketch out in speaking the ancient misfortunes and invented griefs of heroes, and who am not the actor of another's part but the author of my own, when Manius
passages.notes: The sentence is incomplete; it continues in the following context (Aquilius had to be kept in the state). "M’." is the abbreviation for Manius.

passages.original: dicere enim aiunt Ennium, flammam a sapiente facilius ore in ardente opprimi, quam bona dicta teneat; haec scilicet bona dicta, quae salsa sint; nam ea dicta appellantur proprio iam nomine. Sed ut in Scaevola continuit ea Crassus atque in illo altero genere, in quo nulli aculei contumeliarum inerant, causam illam disputationemque elusit, sic in Bruto, quem oderat et quem dignum contumelia iudicabat, utroque genere pugnavit.
passages.english: For they say Ennius says that a flame is more easily held in a burning mouth by a wise man than good sayings kept back; these 'good sayings' being, of course, the witty ones, for such sayings are now called by that very name. But just as in the case of Scaevola Crassus held these back and, in that other kind in which there were no stings of insult, made sport of that case and argument, so against Brutus, whom he hated and judged deserving of insult, he fought with both kinds.

passages.original: ut in illum Titium, qui cum studiose pila luderet et idem signa sacra noctu frangere putaretur gregalesque eum, cum in campum non venisset, requirerent, excusavit Vespa Terentius, quod eum bracchium fregisse diceret; ut illud Africani, quod est apud Lucilium Quid Decius? Nuculam an confixum vis facere? inquit:
passages.english: as against that Titius, who was a keen ball-player and was also thought to break sacred statues at night, and when his companions missed him because he had not come to the Campus, Vespa Terentius excused him by saying that he had broken an arm; or that saying of Africanus which is in Lucilius: "What of Decius? Do you want to make a 'Nucula' or a pierced one?" he says:
passages.notes: The Lucilius quotation is obscure and probably corrupt as transmitted; the pun on "Nucula" (little nut, also a cognomen) cannot be reconstructed with confidence.

passages.original: ut ego nuper Nummium divisorem, ut Neoptolemum ad Troiam, sic illum in campo Martio nomen invenisse; atque haec omnia verbo continentur. Saepe etiam versus facete interponitur, vel ut est vel paululum immutatus, aut aliqua pars versus, ut Stati a Scauro stomachante; ex quo sunt non nulli, qui tuam legem de civitate natam, Crasse, dicant: st, tacete, quid hoc clamoris? Quibus nec mater nec pater,tanta confidentia? Auferte istam enim superbiam.
passages.english: as I recently said that Nummius the bribe-distributor had found his name on the Campus Martius, as Neoptolemus had found his at Troy; and all of this is contained in a single word. Often too a line of verse is wittily inserted, either as it stands or slightly altered, or some part of a line, as [a line] of Statius [was quoted] by Scaurus in a fit of temper; from which there are some who say that your law on citizenship, Crassus, was born: "Hush, be quiet! What is this shouting? You who have neither mother nor father, such boldness? Away with that arrogance!"
passages.notes: The joke on Nummius depends on Latin nummus, "coin" (a bribe-agent named from money), as Neoptolemus ("new war") was named from his first service. "Stati" probably refers to the comic poet Caecilius Statius. The verse quotation is cited loosely; the line division is uncertain.

passages.original: ornant igitur in primis orationem verba relata contrarie, quod idem genus saepe est etiam facetum, ut Servius ille Galba cum iudices L. Scribonio tribuno plebis ferret familiaris suos et dixisset Libo quando tandem, Galba, de triclinio tuo exibis?cum tu inquit de cubiculo alieno. A quo genere ne illud quidem plurimum distat, quod Glaucia Metello villam in Tiburti habes, cortem in Palatio.
passages.english: Words set in contrast, then, are an especial ornament of speech, and this same kind is often also witty: as when the well-known Servius Galba was proposing his own intimates as judges to Lucius Scribonius, tribune of the plebs, and Libo had said, "When, Galba, will you ever come out of your dining room?" he replied, "When you come out of other men's bedrooms." Not very far from this kind is that saying of Glaucia to Metellus: "You have a villa at Tibur, a farmyard on the Palatine."

passages.original: Et hercule omnia haec, quae a me de facetiis disputantur, non maiora forensium actionum quam omnium sermonum condimenta sunt. Nam sicut quod apud Catonem est—qui multa rettulit, ex quibus a me exempli causa non nulla ponuntur—per mihi scitum videtur, C. Publicium solitum dicere P. Mummium cuiusvis temporis hominem esse, sic profecto se res habet, nullum ut sit vitae tempus, in quo non deceat leporem humanitatemque versari.
passages.english: And, by Hercules, all these things I am discussing about wit are no more the seasoning of speeches in court than of all conversation. For just as the remark in Cato (who recorded many sayings, some of which I am setting down as examples) seems to me very clever, that Gaius Publicius used to say that Publius Mummius was a man for any occasion, so surely the case stands, that there is no occasion in life in which charm and refinement are not fitting.

passages.original: ut illud Nasicae, qui cum ad poetam Ennium venisset eique ab ostio quaerenti Ennium ancilla dixisset domi non esse, Nasica sensit illam domini iussu dixisse et illum intus esse; paucis post diebus cum ad Nasicam venisset Ennius et eum ad ianuam quaereret, exclamat Nasica domi non esse, tum Ennius quid? ego non cognosco vocem inquit tuam? Hic Nasica homo es impudens: ego cum te quaererem ancillae tuae credidi te domi non esse, tu mihi non credis ipsi? Est bellum illud quoque, ex quo is, qui dixit inridetur in eo ipso genere, quo dixit;
passages.english: like that of Nasica, who, when he had come to the poet Ennius and, as he asked for Ennius at the door, the maid had told him he was not at home, Nasica realised that she had said it on her master's orders and that he was inside; a few days later, when Ennius had come to Nasica and was asking for him at the door, Nasica shouts that he is not at home. Then Ennius says, "What? Don't I recognise your voice?" At this Nasica: "You are a shameless man: when I was looking for you I believed your maid that you were not at home; do you not believe me myself?" That kind is also pleasant in which the one who said something is mocked in the very same kind in which he said it;

passages.original: tum enim non sal, sed natura ridetur; in quo, ut mihi videtur, persalsum illud est apud Novium: quid ploras, pater?Mirum ni cantem: condemnatus sum. Huic generi quasi contrarium est ridiculi genus patientis ac lenti, ut, cum Cato percussus esset ab eo, qui arcam ferebat, cum ille diceret cave, rogavit num quid aliud ferret praeter arcam.
passages.english: for then it is not wit that is laughed at, but character; in this kind, as it seems to me, that line in Novius is very witty: "Why are you weeping, father?" "It would be a wonder if I were singing: I have been condemned." Contrary, as it were, to this kind is the kind of humour that is patient and unhurried, as when Cato was struck by a man carrying a chest, and the man said "Look out!", he asked whether he was carrying anything else besides the chest.

passages.original: Cuius est vel maxime insigne illud exemplum, ut ceteras artis omittamus, quod dicebat Isocrates doctor singularis se calcaribus in Ephoro, contra autem in Theopompo frenis uti solere: alterum enim exsultantem verborum audacia reprimebat alterum cunctantem et quasi verecundantem incitabat.
passages.english: Of this the most striking example of all, to pass over the other arts, is what Isocrates, that remarkable teacher, used to say: that he was accustomed to use spurs on Ephorus but, on the other hand, the reins on Theopompus; for the one, who ran riot in boldness of language, he held back, and the other, who hesitated and was as it were bashful, he urged on.

passages.original: Equidem cum audio socrum meam Laeliam—facilius enim mulieres incorruptam antiquitatem conservant, quod multorum sermonis expertes ea tenent semper, quae prima didicerunt—sed eam sic audio, ut Plautum mihi aut Naevium videar audire, sono ipso vocis ita recto et simplici est, ut nihil ostentationis aut imitationis adferre videatur; ex quo sic locutum esse eius patrem iudico, sic maiores; non aspere ut ille, quem dixi, non vaste, non rustice, non hiulce, sed presse et aequabiliter et leniter.
passages.english: For my part, when I hear my mother-in-law Laelia (for women more easily preserve uncorrupted antiquity, because, having no share in the conversation of many people, they always keep what they first learned), but I hear her in such a way that I seem to myself to be hearing Plautus or Naevius; in the very sound of her voice she is so straightforward and simple that she seems to bring in nothing of display or affectation; from which I judge that her father spoke thus, and her ancestors thus; not harshly like the man I mentioned, not broadly, not rustically, not with gaping vowels, but concisely, evenly and smoothly.
passages.notes: The sentence is broken off after the parenthesis and resumed with "sed", as in the Latin.

passages.original: hinc illi Lycurgi, hinc Pittaci, hinc Solones atque ab hac similitudine Coruncanii nostri, Fabricii, Catones, Scipiones fuerunt, non tam fortasse docti, sed impetu mentis simili et voluntate. Eadem autem alii prudentia, sed consilio ad vitae studia dispari quietem atque otium secuti, ut Pythagoras, Democritus, Anaxagoras, a regendis civitatibus totos se ad cognitionem rerum transtulerunt; quae vita propter tranquillitatem et propter ipsius scientiae suavitatem, qua nihil est hominibus iucundius, pluris, quam utile fuit rebus publicis, delectavit.
passages.english: hence came those Lycurguses, hence the Pittacuses, hence the Solons, and on this model our own Coruncaniuses, Fabriciuses, Catos and Scipios, perhaps not so learned, but alike in impulse of mind and in will. Others, however, of the same wisdom but with a different plan for their life's pursuits, followed quiet and leisure, like Pythagoras, Democritus and Anaxagoras, and transferred themselves wholly from governing states to the study of nature; and this life, because of its tranquillity and the sweetness of knowledge itself, than which nothing is more delightful to human beings, attracted more people than was useful for the commonwealth.

passages.original: Itaque, ut ei studio se excellentissimis ingeniis homines dediderunt, ex ea summa facultate vacui ac liberi temporis multo plura, quam erat necesse, doctissimi homines otio nimio et ingeniis uberrimis adfluentes curanda sibi esse ac quaerenda et investiganda duxerunt. Nam vetus quidem illa doctrina eadem videtur et recte faciendi et bene dicendi magistra; neque disiuncti doctores, sed eidem erant vivendi praeceptores atque dicendi, ut ille apud Homerum Phoenix, qui se a Peleo patre Achilli iuveni comitem esse datum dicit ad bellum, ut efficeret oratorem verborum actoremque rerum.
passages.english: And so, as men of the most outstanding talents gave themselves to that pursuit, out of that great abundance of free and unoccupied time, these most learned men, overflowing with excessive leisure and the richest talents, thought that they must attend to, inquire into and investigate many more things than was necessary. For that old learning seems to have been the same teacher both of right action and of good speaking; nor were the teachers separate, but the same men were instructors in living and in speaking, like that Phoenix in Homer, who says that he was given by Peleus, his father, as a companion to the young Achilles for the war, to make him a speaker of words and a doer of deeds.

passages.original: quorum princeps Socrates fuit, is qui omnium eruditorum testimonio totiusque iudicio Graeciae cum prudentia et acumine et venustate et subtilitate tum vero eloquentia, varietate, copia, quam se cumque in partem dedisset omnium fuit facile princeps, eisque, qui haec, quae nunc nos quaerimus, tractarent, agerent, docerent, cum nomine appellarentur uno, quod omnis rerum optimarum cognitio atque in eis exercitatio philosophia nominaretur, hoc commune nomen eripuit sapienterque sentiendi et ornate dicendi scientiam re cohaerentis disputationibus suis separavit; cuius ingenium variosque sermones immortalitati scriptis suis Plato tradidit, cum ipse litteram Socrates nullam reliquisset.
passages.english: Their leader was Socrates, the man who, by the testimony of all the learned and the judgment of all Greece, was easily the foremost of all, not only in wisdom, acuteness, charm and subtlety, but also in eloquence, variety and fullness, in whatever direction he turned himself; and though those who handled, practised and taught these things which we are now investigating were called by one name, because all knowledge of the best things and practice in them was called philosophy, he stripped them of this common name, and in his discussions separated the science of thinking wisely and that of speaking elegantly, which are in reality joined together; his genius and varied conversations Plato handed down to immortality in his writings, since Socrates himself had left not a single letter.

passages.original: Ac, si quaeris, Catule, de doctrina ista quid ego sentiam, non tantum ingenioso homini et ei, qui forum, qui curiam, qui causas, qui rem publicam spectet, opus esse arbitror temporis, quantum sibi ei sumpserunt, quos discentis vita defecit: omnes enim artes aliter ab eis tractantur, qui eas ad usum transferunt, aliter ab eis, qui ipsarum artium tractatu delectati nihil in vita sunt aliud acturi. Magister hic Samnitium summa iam senectute est et cotidie commentatur, nihil enim curat aliud: at Q. Velocius puer addidicerat, sed quod erat aptus ad illud totumque cognorat, fuit, ut est apud Lucilium, quamvis bonus ipse Samnis in ludo ac rudibus cuivis satis asper; sed plus operae foro tribuebat, amicis, rei familiari. Valerius cotidie cantabat; erat enim scaenicus: quid faceret aliud?
passages.english: And, if you ask, Catulus, what I think about that learning, I do not consider that a talented man, one who has an eye to the forum, the senate house, the courts and public affairs, needs as much time as those have taken for themselves whom life has failed while they were still learning; for all arts are handled one way by those who apply them to use, another way by those who, delighted by the handling of the arts themselves, will do nothing else in life. This trainer of Samnites is now in extreme old age and practises every day, for he cares for nothing else; but Quintus Velocius had learned it as a boy, and because he was suited to it and had mastered it wholly, he was, as Lucilius has it, 'though himself a good Samnite in the school and with the wooden foils, rough enough for anyone'; but he gave more effort to the forum, to his friends, to his estate. Valerius sang every day; for he was an actor: what else was he to do?
passages.notes: "Samnites" here are a class of gladiators. The Lucilius quotation is somewhat uncertain in sense.

passages.original: Ipse ille Leontinus Gorgias, quo patrono, ut Plato voluit, philosopho succubuit orator, qui aut non est victus umquam a Socrate neque sermo ille Platonis verus est; aut, si est victus, eloquentior videlicet fuit et disertior Socrates et, ut tu appellas, copiosior et melior orator—sed hic in illo ipso Platonis libro de omni re, quaecumque in disceptationem quaestionemque vocetur, se copiosissime dicturum esse profitetur;
passages.english: That very Gorgias of Leontini, with whom as his champion, as Plato would have it, the orator was overcome by the philosopher; who either was never defeated by Socrates, and that dialogue of Plato is not true; or, if he was defeated, then evidently Socrates was more eloquent and more skilful in speech and, as you call it, a fuller and better orator; but this man, in that very book of Plato, professes that he will speak most fully on any subject whatever that is brought up for discussion and inquiry;
passages.notes: The sentence is anacoluthic; the subject "Gorgias" is resumed by "hic".

passages.original: Hic Sulpicius ego vero, inquit Crasse, neque Aristotelem istum neque Carneadem nec philosophorum quemquam desidero. Vel me licet existimes desperare ista posse perdiscere vel, id quod facio, contemnere; mihi rerum forensium et communium vulgaris haec cognitio satis magna est ad eam, quam specto, eloquentiam;
passages.english: At this point Sulpicius said, "For my part, Crassus, I feel no need of that Aristotle of yours, nor of Carneades, nor of any of the philosophers. You may suppose either that I despair of being able to learn those things thoroughly or, as is the case, that I despise them; for me this common knowledge of forensic and public affairs is great enough for the eloquence I aim at;

passages.original: Conlocationis est componere et struere verba sic, ut neve asper eorum concursus neve hiulcus sit, sed quodam modo coagmentatus et levis; in quo lepide soceri mei persona lusit is, qui elegantissime id facere potuit, Lucilius: quam lepide λέξεις compostae! ut tesserulae omnes arte pavimento atque emblemate vermiculato. Quae cum dixisset in Albucium inludens, ne a me quidem abstinuit: Crassum habeo generum, ne rhetoricoterus tu sis.
passages.english: It belongs to arrangement to put together and build up the words in such a way that their meeting is neither harsh nor gaping, but in a certain manner fitted together and smooth. On this point the man who was able to do it most elegantly, Lucilius, made fun charmingly in the person of my father-in-law: "How charmingly the *lexeis* [phrases] are put together! Like all the little tiles, set with skill in a pavement and a mosaic inlay of wormlike pattern." And when he had said this, mocking Albucius, he did not spare even me: "I have Crassus as son-in-law; don't you be too much of a rhetorician."
passages.notes: The speaker is Crassus; the father-in-law whose persona Lucilius adopts is Q. Mucius Scaevola (the Augur), named only by implication here. The Lucilius verses are quoted in Greek-tinged wording: λέξεις ("phrases, words") and "rhetoricoterus" (a Latinized Greek comparative, "more rhetorical"). The sense of the last line is disputed; it may mean "I have Crassus as son-in-law, lest you be the more rhetorical one" or "so do not be too rhetorical." "Emblemate vermiculato" refers to fine mosaic work in sinuous, worm-like lines (opus vermiculatum).

passages.original: quos necessitas cogit et ipsi numeri ac modi sic verba versu includere, ut nihil sit ne spiritu quidem minimo brevius aut longius, quam necesse est. Liberior est oratio et plane, ut dicitur, sic est vere soluta, non ut fugiat tamen aut erret, sed ut sine vinculis sibi ipsa moderetur. Namque ego illud adsentior Theophrasto, qui putat orationem, quae quidem sit polita atque facta quodam modo, non astricte, sed remissius numerosam esse oportere.
passages.english: [poets,] whom necessity and the rhythms and measures themselves compel to enclose their words in verse in such a way that nothing is even by the smallest breath shorter or longer than is necessary. Prose is freer, and is plainly, as it is called, truly 'loosed', yet not so that it runs off or wanders, but so that without fetters it governs itself. For I agree with Theophrastus, who thinks that prose, at least prose that is polished and in some way crafted, ought to be rhythmical, not strictly, but in a looser way.
passages.notes: 'soluta' (loosed, unbound) plays on 'oratio soluta', the Latin term for prose.

passages.original: animi est enim omnis actio et imago animi vultus, indices oculi: nam haec est una pars corporis, quae, quot animi motus sunt, tot significationes et commutationes possit efficere; neque vero est quisquam qui eadem conivens efficiat. Theophrastus quidem Tauriscum quendam dicit actorem aversum solitum esse dicere, qui in agendo contuens aliquid pronuntiaret.
passages.english: for all delivery is of the mind, and the face is the image of the mind, the eyes its indicators: for this is the one part of the body that can produce as many signs and changes as there are movements of the mind; and indeed there is no one who can produce the same effects with his eyes shut. Theophrastus indeed says that a certain Tauriscus used to say that an actor who delivered his lines while staring fixedly at something was [speaking with his] back turned.
passages.notes: The sense of the last sentence is debated: 'aversum' (turned away) is usually taken as the predicate describing an actor who fixes his gaze on one point while speaking, i.e. as if he were addressing the audience with his back to them. Tauriscus is otherwise unidentified.
